quotes.verbatim_quote:
We can use 3 different quartal chord families over a"D" half diminished chord. Two of them
  are derived from two different major scales: “Eb” major and “Db” major, and the last one is
  derived from a melodic minor scale: F melodic minor.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This establishes the foundational rule for choosing quartal chord families over a half-diminished chord, specifying the three source scales.

quotes.topic: Db major quartal as blues/tritone substitution
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The “Eb” major quartal chord family brings the locrian sound to Dø. However the "Db"
  major quartal family is quite "tricky" because we transformed the Dø into D7(#9) chord,
  giving it a blues vibe. Then using the tritone substitution for D7(#9), we can Aind Ab7(13),
  that we can consider mixolydian. Therefore, having this mixolydian chord, we can Aind the
  "Db" major scale quartal chord voicings.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This explains the harmonic transformation chain—half-diminished to dominant 7(#9) to tritone sub—that justifies using Db major quartal voicings, a core analytical move of the method.

quotes.topic: lower note caution in quartal voicings
quotes.verbatim_quote: Note: Be careful of the lower notes. They can make the chord sound undesirable.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is a direct rule of thumb about voice-leading and register when applying quartal voicings, alerting the player to a common pitfall.

quotes.topic: D half-diminished as VI of F melodic minor
quotes.verbatim_quote:
As we know the Dø chord is the VI degree of F melodic minor. Therefore, we can use the F
  melodic minor quartal chord voicings over it.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the modal relationship that licenses use of F melodic minor quartal voicings over D half-diminished, a key conceptual link.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The first degree of "F" melodic minor quartal chord family [Fm(maj7) add4] sometimes can be
  replaced by a chord not belonging to that family: D#/E, which is actually a F#7 (13) b9 over E.
  This is not a rule, it is just a chord voicing that works well with the other voicings even though
  it does not belong to this chord family.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives an explicit exception to the chord-family system, showing that practical voice-leading can override theoretical family membership.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
As a matter of fact, some chords on the lower strings might not sound desirable, in these cases
we can take out the lower note and play a 3 note quartal voicing.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This provides a concrete remediation technique—dropping the lowest note—for quartal voicings that sound muddy on lower strings.

quotes.topic: dorian quartal over static/modal interchange harmonies
quotes.verbatim_quote:
Usually the dorian chords are related to static harmonies. However, they can be a
  tremendous asset when used over non traditional harmonic situations, giving a dorian
  modal vibe to the chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the primary use-case for dorian quartal voicings and opens the door to their application in modal interchange contexts.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A dominant chord that is used incorrectly most of the time is the lydian dominant (also
  called mixolydian #4). It can only be used over dominant 7th chords that are not leading to
  any other chord. The only exception is when we have a sequence of many dominant 7th
  chords one after another
quotes.why_load_bearing: This states a strict prescriptive rule about when the lydian dominant voicing is and is not appropriate, directly governing its application in II/V/I contexts.

quotes.topic: mixolydian voicings: major vs. minor cadence rule
quotes.verbatim_quote:
On the Vth degree of a minor cadence, we can use all the possibilities we have learned for
  dominant 7th chords, except with the mixolydian chord voicings, which can only be used
  when they are leading to major chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is a critical restriction rule distinguishing which dominant voicing families are available over the V chord in minor vs. major cadences.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The following exercises on the next page contain:

1) Triads
2) Tetrads
3) Quartal Chords
4) Chord Inversions
5) Tritone Substitutions
quotes.why_load_bearing: This explicitly enumerates the five harmonic devices combined in the extended block chord section, defining the vocabulary of the chapter's exercises.

quotes.topic: memorize vs. analyze block chord ideas
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The following block chord ideas are great examples of giving us a better idea of how to
                            68


build our own ideas, using the concepts we have been learning up until now. But
remember they should be memorized and not just analyzed in order to become natural
and easy to play.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is a pedagogical rule distinguishing the method's expectation—internalization through memorization—from mere intellectual analysis of the examples.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
It is important to understand that we will be learning two different things at the same
time: chord ideas and rhythmic ideas which we will call "groove ideas". Therefore we can
use block chords applying another groove (rhythm) or use one of the groove ideas
extracted from one of the examples but apply different chords.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the method's separation of harmonic content from rhythmic content, establishing that chords and grooves are independently interchangeable variables.

quotes.topic: improving rhythmic ideas: Big Band listening
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The best thing we can do is to listen to "Big Bands" as often as possible, because the
"grooves" are very clear and easy to understand. However, in order to make them become
part of us, we should memorize the songs we like, always singing with the recordings.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This gives the method's prescribed practice technique for internalizing groove vocabulary: active listening and singing along with Big Band recordings.
